title: Der Hahnenbalken
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 149. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng).
about: KHM 149 opens with a traveling conjurer whose crowd is fooled into seeing a rooster carry a heavy beam — a Hahnenbalken is the timber laid across a roof-ridge to hold a weathercock — when really it is only a straw. A sharp-eyed girl breaks the illusion and the conjurer is driven off in disgrace, but he keeps his promise of revenge: at her wedding he tricks her into wading, in her finery, through what looks like a flooded stream but is really a field of blooming flax. It's a short story about eyes that trust too easily, and a grudge that waits.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Zauberer, der stand mitten in einer großen Menge Volks und vollbrachte seine Wunderdinge.
sentences.l: There was once a sorcerer, who stood in the middle of a great crowd of people and accomplished his wonder-works.
sentences.i: There was once a sorcerer who stood in the midst of a great throng of people and performed his marvels.
sentences.n: “Es war einmal” is the standing opening of these tales — “there was once.” “Menge Volks” keeps the old genitive after a word of quantity, where modern German would simply say “Menge Volk.”

sentences.t: Da ließ er auch einen Hahn einherschreiten, der hob einen schweren Balken und trug ihn als wäre er federleicht.
sentences.l: There he also let a cock stride along, which lifted a heavy beam and carried it as though it were light-as-a-feather.
sentences.i: Among his tricks he had a cock come pacing out, and it lifted a heavy beam and carried it as though it weighed no more than a feather.
sentences.n: “ließ … einherschreiten” — lassen with an infinitive means to have something done: the conjuror does not walk, he makes the cock walk. “einherschreiten” is a stately verb, to pace solemnly along. “federleicht” glues Feder ‘feather’ to leicht ‘light.’

sentences.t: Nun war aber ein Mädchen, das hatte eben ein vierblättriges Kleeblatt gefunden und war dadurch klug geworden, so daß kein Blendwerk vor ihm bestehen konnte,
sentences.l: Now there was however a girl, she had just found a four-leaved clover-leaf and had thereby become clever, so that no illusion could hold up before her,
sentences.i: Now there was a girl who had just found a four-leaved clover and had been made clear-sighted by it, so that no illusion could stand up before her,
sentences.n: Both “das” and “ihm” refer back to das Mädchen, which is grammatically neuter; German keeps the neuter forms all through, and English has to say “she” and “her.” Folk belief held that a four-leaved clover let whoever carried it see through enchantment; the tale states this flatly and explains nothing.

sentences.t: und sah daß der Balken nichts war als ein Strohhalm.
sentences.l: and saw that the beam was nothing but a straw.
sentences.i: and she saw that the beam was nothing but a wisp of straw.
sentences.n: “nichts … als” = nothing but. The subject is simply carried over from the clause before — German can leave “sie” out here, English cannot.

sentences.t: Da rief es „ihr Leute, seht ihr nicht, das ist ein bloßer Strohhalm und kein Balken, was der Hahn da trägt.“
sentences.l: Then it called “you people, do you not see, that is a mere straw and no beam, what the cock is carrying there.”
sentences.i: Then she cried, “Good people, do you not see — that is a mere straw and no beam, what the cock is carrying there.”
sentences.n: “es” is the girl again. The shout has the shape of spoken word order: the claim first, and the thing it is about (“was der Hahn da trägt”) trailing after it. The 1857 text closes the outburst with a full stop, not a question mark.

sentences.t: Alsbald verschwand der Zauber, und die Leute sahen was es war und jagten den Hexenmeister mit Schimpf und Schande fort.
sentences.l: At once the enchantment vanished, and the people saw what it was and drove the sorcerer away with insult and disgrace.
sentences.i: At once the spell broke, and the people saw what it truly was, and drove the wizard off with abuse and disgrace.
sentences.n: “jagten … fort” is fortjagen, to chase away, with the particle held to the end of the clause. “Hexenmeister” — Hexe ‘witch’ plus Meister ‘master’ — is a harsher name for him than the “Zauberer” of the opening line.

sentences.t: Er aber, voll innerlichen Zornes, sprach „ich will mich schon rächen.“
sentences.l: He however, full of inward rage, said “I will avenge myself, never fear.”
sentences.i: But he, full of inward rage, said, “I shall have my revenge yet.”
sentences.n: “voll innerlichen Zornes” takes the genitive after voll, the older construction. “schon” here is not ‘already’ but the particle of confident assurance — ‘never fear,’ ‘you will see.’

sentences.t: Nach einiger Zeit hielt das Mädchen Hochzeit, war geputzt und gieng in einem großen Zug über das Feld nach dem Ort, wo die Kirche stand.
sentences.l: After some time the girl held her wedding, was decked out and went in a great procession over the field toward the place where the church stood.
sentences.i: After a time the girl held her wedding; she was decked out and went in a great procession across the field toward the place where the church stood.
sentences.n: “hielt Hochzeit” — Hochzeit halten is the set phrase for holding a wedding. “Zug” here is a procession, the bridal train, not the ‘pull’ or ‘draught’ the word carries elsewhere.

sentences.t: Auf einmal kamen sie an einen stark angeschwollenen Bach, und war keine Brücke und kein Steg, darüber zu gehen.
sentences.l: All at once they came to a strongly swollen brook, and [there] was no bridge and no footbridge to go over it.
sentences.i: All at once they came upon a brook swollen high, and there was no bridge and no plank to cross by.
sentences.n: “und war keine Brücke” has no subject at all: German may leave the “es” out after und, so the English supplies it in square brackets. A “Steg” is the plank or narrow footbridge a village keeps over its stream.

sentences.t: Da war die Braut flink, hob ihre Kleider auf und wollte durchwaten.
sentences.l: Then the bride was quick, lifted her clothes up and wanted to wade through.
sentences.i: Then the bride, quick about it, gathered her skirts up and made to wade across.
sentences.n: “hob … auf” is aufheben, to lift up, split around its object. “durchwaten” is durch- plus waten, to wade through.

sentences.t: Wie sie nun eben im Wasser so steht, ruft ein Mann, und das war der Zauberer, neben ihr ganz spöttisch „ei! wo hast du deine Augen, daß du das für ein Wasser hältst?“
sentences.l: As she now just stands so in the water, a man calls, and that was the sorcerer, beside her quite mockingly “eh! where do you have your eyes, that you take that for water?”
sentences.i: Just as she is standing there in the water, a man calls out beside her, quite mockingly — and it was the sorcerer — “Ah! where are your eyes, that you take that for water?”
sentences.n: The tale slips into the present tense (“steht,” “ruft”) for the moment of the trap and drops back into the past afterwards; German narrative does this for vividness. “für … halten” is to take something for something — not ‘to hold.’

sentences.t: Da giengen ihr die Augen auf, und sie sah daß sie mit ihren aufgehobenen Kleidern mitten in einem blaublühenden Flachsfeld stand.
sentences.l: Then the eyes went open to her, and she saw that she with her lifted-up clothes stood in the middle of a blue-flowering flax-field.
sentences.i: Then her eyes were opened, and she saw that she was standing with her skirts held up in the middle of a flax field in blue flower.
sentences.n: “giengen ihr die Augen auf” is a dative of possession: the eyes belong to her, so German says the eyes went open ‘to her.’ The verb is aufgehen, split as “giengen … auf.” Flax in bloom is a sheet of pale blue, which is what lets it pass for water.

sentences.t: Da sahen es die Leute auch allesammt und jagten sie mit Schimpf und Gelächter fort.
sentences.l: Then the people all together saw it too and drove her away with insult and laughter.
sentences.i: Then the people all saw it too, and drove her off with abuse and laughter.
sentences.n: The last line answers the fifth almost word for word — “mit Schimpf und Schande fort” against “mit Schimpf und Gelächter fort” — so that her disgrace matches his exactly. That balance is the whole of the tale.

glossary.es: es — it (here also ‘she’, since das Mädchen is neuter; and the impersonal subject, as in „Es war einmal“ = there was once)
glossary.hob: heben — lifted, raised (3rd sg. past); with auf: hob … auf = lifted up, picked up
glossary.hältst: halten — you hold (2nd sg. pres.); halten für = to take (something) for
glossary.jagten: jagen — chased, drove (3rd pl. past); fortjagen = to drive away
glossary.zug: der Zug — procession, train of people (also a pull, a draught)
